The packing fraction measures how far the **atomic mass** departs from the whole number
**A**, per nucleon.
**Step 1 — state the definition.**
**packing fraction f = (M − A)/A** ✓
where M is the atomic mass in **atomic mass units** and A the mass number.
**Step 2 — see what it measures.** M − A is the **mass defect** expressed relative to
the whole-number mass ✓ Dividing by A gives the departure **per nucleon**, which is
what makes different nuclides comparable.
**Why the quantity is usually negative.** For stable nuclei the actual mass is **less**
than A u, because binding energy has been released ✓ so M − A < 0 and the packing
fraction is negative. It is often quoted multiplied by 10⁴ for convenience.
**How it relates to stability.** A **more negative** packing fraction means a more
tightly bound nucleus ✓ The curve of f against A dips to a minimum near **A = 56**,
iron - exactly where the binding energy per nucleon peaks. Iron is the most stable
nuclide, which is why stellar fusion stops there.
**The two ends of the curve.**
very **light** nuclei: f is positive or near zero - loosely bound, so **fusion**
releases energy ✓
very **heavy** nuclei: f rises again towards zero - so **fission** releases energy ✓
Both nuclear power and stellar energy follow from the shape of this curve.
**A worked instance.** For ¹⁶O, the atomic mass is **15·9949 u**:
f = (15·9949 − 16)/16 = **−3·2 x 10⁻⁴** ✓ and multiplied by 10⁴ it is quoted as −3·2.
**Why A is the natural divisor.** It counts the nucleons ✓ A nucleus with twice as many
nucleons would have roughly twice the total mass defect, so dividing by A removes the
size and leaves a measure of **quality** of binding.
**The related quantity.** The **binding energy per nucleon**, B/A, carries the same
information with the opposite sign convention ✓ and is the more common modern measure.
**Reading the distractors.** **A/(M − A)** ✗ is the reciprocal. **(A − M)/A** ✗ has the
sign reversed, making stable nuclei positive. **M/(M − A)** ✗ matches no definition ✓
∴ (M − A)/A.

Count how many times the activity has **halved**.
**Step 1 — find the ratio of the counts.**
240/30 = **8** ✓
**Step 2 — express 8 as a power of two.**
8 = **2³** ✓
so the activity has halved **three** times.
**Step 3 — divide the elapsed time.** One hour = 60 minutes covers three half-lives:
T₁/₂ = 60/3
= **20 minutes** ✓
**Step 4 — check the sequence.**
at 0 min: **240** counts per minute
at 20 min: **120**
at 40 min: **60**
at 60 min: **30** ✓ exactly as observed.
**Why the count rate tracks the number of nuclei.** Activity is
A = λN ✓
so the measured count rate is proportional to how many undecayed nuclei remain. Halving
the count rate means halving the number of nuclei.
**The formal route.**
N = N₀(½)^(t/T)
30/240 = (½)^(60/T)
(½)³ = (½)^(60/T)
60/T = 3, so **T = 20 min** ✓
**Why no calculus is needed.** Whenever the ratio is a neat power of two, simply
counting halvings is quickest ✓ For an awkward ratio one would use
T = 0·693t/ln(N₀/N).
**The decay constant.**
λ = 0·693/T = 0·693/20 = **0·0347 min⁻¹** ✓
and the **mean life** is 1/λ = **28·9 min**, always longer than the half-life by the
factor 1/0·693 = 1·44.
**Why the background is ignored.** A real measurement would subtract the background
count ✓ The question gives clean figures, so no correction is implied.
**Reading the distractors.** **30 min** ✗ would leave 240/4 = 60 cpm after an hour.
**80 min** ✗ and **120 min** ✗ are even slower, giving 143 and 170 cpm ✓ Only a 20-minute
half-life brings 240 down to 30 in an hour.
∴ 20 min.

The half-life is **0·693** times the mean life.
**Step 1 — recall the relation.**
mean life τ = 1/λ
half-life T₁/₂ = 0·693/λ ✓
so
**T₁/₂ = 0·693 τ** ✓
**Step 2 — convert the mean life to minutes.**
100 s = 100/60
= **1·667 min** ✓
**Step 3 — multiply.**
T₁/₂ = 0·693 x 1·667
= **1·155 min** ✓
**Why the half-life is shorter than the mean life.** The decay is exponential, with a
long thin tail ✓ A few nuclei survive a very long time and drag the **average** upward,
while **half** the sample has already gone by 0·693τ. The mean is always the larger, by
the factor 1/0·693 = **1·44**.
**Where the 0·693 comes from.** It is **ln 2** ✓
N = N₀e^(−λt), and setting N = N₀/2 gives λt = ln 2, so t = **0·693/λ**.
**The meaning of the mean life.** The average time a nucleus survives before decaying ✓
It is also the time for the activity to fall to **1/e = 37%** of its initial value,
against 50% at the half-life.
**A check by the exponential.** After 1·155 min = 69·3 s:
N/N₀ = e^(−69·3/100) = e^(−0·693) = **0·5** ✓ exactly half, confirming the answer.
**Watch the units.** The question gives seconds and asks for **minutes** ✓ Answering
69·3 - correct in seconds - would miss the conversion, and neither 69·3 nor 1·155 would
be confused if the units were not switched deliberately.
**The three time constants, compared.**
**mean life** τ = 1/λ: 100 s = **1·667 min**
**half-life** 0·693τ: **1·155 min** ✓
**time to fall to 1/10**: 2·303τ = **3·84 min**
**Reading the distractors.** **0·693** ✗ is the conversion factor itself, as if the mean
life were 1 minute. **1** ✗ and **10⁻⁴** ✗ match no step ✓
∴ 1.155.

Radioactive decay is a **random** process with **no memory** - a nucleus does not age.
**Step 1 — state the law.** Every undecayed nucleus of a given nuclide has the **same**
probability λ dt of decaying in the next interval dt ✓ regardless of how long it has
already existed.
**Step 2 — apply it to the two nuclei.** One was made five billion years ago, the other
five minutes ago, but **both are identical nuclei of the same nuclide** ✓ so their decay
probabilities in the next interval are **the same**.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The probability is **independent of the time of creation** ✓
**Why nuclei do not age.** A nucleus has no internal clock, no accumulating wear, no
memory of its history ✓ It is a quantum system in a definite state, and decay is a
spontaneous quantum transition whose rate depends only on the state. This is called the
**memoryless** property.
**The contrast with human mortality.** A person's chance of dying next year rises
steeply with age ✓ A nucleus's does not. If people behaved like nuclei, a 90-year-old
would be no more likely to die next year than a 20-year-old - and the survivors would
follow a pure exponential curve.
**How the exponential law follows.** A constant decay probability per unit time gives
dN/dt = −λN ✓
whose solution is N = N₀e^(−λt). The exponential is a **consequence** of the
memorylessness, not an extra assumption.
**What the half-life really means.** Not that each nucleus lives that long, but that
**half** the sample survives it ✓ Of the survivors, half will survive another
half-life - and so on, with no change in the odds.
**The practical consequence for dating.** Carbon dating works because the **fraction**
remaining depends only on the elapsed time since the organism died ✓ Not on anything
about the individual atoms, which are all equally likely to go next.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Different for each nucleus**" ✗ assumes nuclei age.
"**The older one decays first**" ✗ and "**the newer one decays first**" ✗ both impose an
order on a process that has none ✓
∴ independent of the time of creation.

An **isotope** of the original element has the **same Z** but a different A - so the
emissions must cancel in charge.
**Step 1 — recall what each emission does.**
**alpha** (⁴₂He): Z falls by **2**, A falls by **4** ✓
**beta** (an electron): Z rises by **1**, A unchanged ✓
**gamma**: neither Z nor A changes
**Step 2 — impose the condition.** For the product to be an isotope of the **original**
element, Z must return to its starting value while A changes ✓
**Step 3 — test one alpha and two betas.**
Z: −2 (alpha) + 1 + 1 (two betas) = **0** ✓ unchanged
A: −4 (alpha) + 0 + 0 = **−4** ✓ changed
So the product has the same Z and a mass number four less - an **isotope** ✓
**Step 4 — check the total.** That is **three** disintegrations, as the question
states ✓
**Step 5 — test the alternatives.**
**2α + 1β**: Z changes by −4 + 1 = **−3** ✗ a different element
**3β**: Z changes by **+3** ✗
**2β + 1γ**: Z changes by **+2** ✗
Only one α and two β returns Z to its original value ✓
**A worked instance.**
²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α
²³⁴₉₀Th → ²³⁴₉₁Pa + β
²³⁴₉₁Pa → ²³⁴₉₂U + β ✓
The chain ends at **²³⁴U**, an isotope of the original ²³⁸U - exactly the pattern
described, and a real segment of the uranium decay series.
**Why this combination recurs in nature.** Alpha decay moves a heavy nucleus **below**
the line of stability in neutron-proton ratio, and the two subsequent beta decays bring
it back ✓ The α-β-β cycle is therefore a common motif in the natural decay chains.
**The order does not matter.** The net changes in Z and A are the same whichever
sequence the three decays occur in ✓
∴ 2β particles and 1α particle.

Nuclear radius goes as **A^(1/3)**, so the volume goes as **A**.
**Step 1 — state the radius formula.**
R = R₀A^(1/3), with R₀ = **1·2 x 10⁻¹⁵ m** ✓
**Step 2 — find the volume.**
V = (4/3)πR³
= (4/3)πR₀³A ✓
so
**V ∝ A** ✓
**What this implies.** The nuclear **density** is
ρ = mass/volume ∝ A/A = **constant** ✓
Every nucleus, from helium to uranium, has essentially the **same density**, about
**2·3 x 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³** - a hundred million million times that of water.
**Why nuclear matter is incompressible.** Nucleons behave rather like closely packed
spheres that touch but do not interpenetrate ✓ Adding more simply makes the nucleus
bigger, not denser - which is why R ∝ A^(1/3) in the first place.
**A worked comparison.**
helium, A = 4: R = 1·2(4)^(1/3) = **1·9 fm**
uranium, A = 238: R = 1·2(238)^(1/3) = **7·4 fm** ✓
Sixty times the mass, but under four times the radius - and the volume ratio is exactly
238/4 = **59·5**, matching the mass ratio as constant density requires.
**Where this density is found elsewhere.** In a **neutron star**, which is in effect a
single enormous nucleus ✓ A teaspoonful would weigh about a billion tonnes.
**How the radius is measured.** By scattering high-energy electrons off nuclei and
analysing the diffraction pattern ✓ Hofstadter won the 1961 Nobel Prize for exactly
this, and it is how R₀ was determined.
**A caution about the "surface".** A nucleus has no sharp edge; the density falls off
over about 2·3 fm ✓ R is defined as the half-density radius, and the A^(1/3) law
describes it well for all but the lightest nuclei.
**Reading the distractors.** **A^(1/3)** ✗ is how the **radius** varies, not the volume.
**A³** ✗ would make the density grow as A², and **√A** ✗ corresponds to no nuclear
relation ✓
∴ A.

An electron is a **lepton** - a fundamental particle that does not feel the strong
force.
**Step 1 — recall the classification.** Matter particles divide into
**leptons**: electron, muon, tau and their three neutrinos - **fundamental**, with no
internal structure, and **not** subject to the strong nuclear force ✓
**hadrons**: particles made of **quarks**, which do feel the strong force
**Step 2 — subdivide the hadrons.**
**baryons**: three quarks - proton, neutron, lambda ✓
**mesons**: a quark and an antiquark - pion, kaon
**Step 3 — place the electron.** It is **point-like** down to the limit of experiment -
below 10⁻¹⁸ m - with no constituents, and it does not participate in the strong
interaction ✓ So it is a **lepton**.
**What the electron does feel.** The **electromagnetic**, **weak** and **gravitational**
forces ✓ but not the strong one - which is precisely why it can orbit a nucleus freely
rather than being drawn into it.
**Why it is not a nucleon.** "Nucleon" means a **proton or neutron**, the constituents
of a nucleus ✓ Electrons are not found in nuclei. The electrons emitted in **beta
decay** are created at the moment of decay, when a neutron turns into a proton; they do
not pre-exist there.
**Why it is not a baryon or hadron.** Both require **quarks** ✓ The electron has none,
and its lepton number of +1 is conserved in every known interaction - which is why an
electron cannot simply turn into a quark.
**The electron's vital statistics.**
mass **9·11 x 10⁻³¹ kg**, or 0·511 MeV/c²
charge **−1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ C**
spin **½**, making it a fermion subject to the Pauli exclusion principle ✓
**Why the exclusion principle matters.** It is why electrons occupy successive shells
rather than all collapsing into the lowest ✓ and therefore why chemistry, the periodic
table and matter as we know it exist at all.
**The discovery.** J. J. Thomson, 1897, from the deflection of cathode rays ✓ the first
**fundamental** particle found, and still fundamental.
∴ A lepton.
